          - paragraph [ref=e196]:
            - text: Haydée Marta Mercedes Sosa Girón (9 July 1935
            - superscript [ref=e197]:
              - link "[1]" [ref=e198] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-birth-1"
            - text: – 4 October 2009) was an Argentine singer who was popular throughout
            - link "Latin America" [ref=e199] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_America
            - text: and many countries outside the region. With her roots in
            - link "Argentine folk music" [ref=e200] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Folk_music_of_Argentina
            - text: ", Sosa became one of the preeminent exponents of"
            - link "El nuevo cancionero" [ref=e201] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nueva_canci%C3%B3n
            - text: . She gave voice to songs written by many Latin American songwriters. She was hailed as the "voice of the voiceless ones",
            - superscript [ref=e202]:
              - link "[2]" [ref=e203] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-tmc-2"
            - text: and often called "the conscience of Latin America".
            - superscript [ref=e204]:
              - link "[3]" [ref=e205] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Heckman-3"
          - paragraph [ref=e206]:
            - text: Sosa performed in venues such as the
            - link "Lincoln Center" [ref=e207] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lincoln_Center
            - text: in New York City, the
            - link "Théâtre Mogador" [ref=e208] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_Mogador
            - text: in Paris, the
            - link "Sistine Chapel" [ref=e209] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sistine_Chapel
            - text: in Vatican City, as well as sold-out shows in New York's
            - link "Carnegie Hall" [ref=e210] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carnegie_Hall
            - text: and the Roman
            - link "Colosseum" [ref=e211] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Colosseum
            - text: during her final decade of life. Her career spanned four decades and she was the recipient of six
            - link "Latin Grammy" [ref=e212] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy
            - text: awards (2000, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2009, 2011), including a
            - link "Latin Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award" [ref=e213] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award
            - text: in 2004 and two posthumous
            - link "Latin Grammy Award for Best Folk Album" [ref=e214] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy_Award_for_Best_Folk_Album
            - text: in 2009 and 2011. She won the
            - link "Premio Gardel" [ref=e215] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Premios_Gardel
            - text: in 2000, the main musical award in Argentina. She served as an ambassador for
            - link "UNICEF" [ref=e216] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/UNICEF
            - text: .
          - generic [ref=e217]:
            - heading "Life" [level=2] [ref=e218]
            - generic [ref=e219]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e220] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Mercedes_Sosa&action=edit&section=1
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e221]:
            - text: Sosa was born on 9 July 1935, in
            - link "San Miguel de Tucumán" [ref=e222] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/San_Miguel_de_Tucum%C3%A1n
            - text: ", in the"
            - link "northwestern Argentine" [ref=e223] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Argentine_Northwest
            - text: province of
            - link "Tucumán" [ref=e224] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Tucum%C3%A1n_Province
            - text: ", of"
            - link "mestizo" [ref=e225] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mestizo
            - text: ancestry. She was of French, Spanish and
            - link "Diaguita" [ref=e226] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Diaguita
            - text: descent.
            - superscript [ref=e227]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e228] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - text: Her nickname "la negra", which is a common nickname in Argentina for people with darker complexion, is a reference to her indigenous heritage.
            - superscript [ref=e229]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e230] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: Her parents, a day laborer and a washerwoman,
            - superscript [ref=e231]:
              - link "[3]" [ref=e232] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Heckman-3"
            - text: were
            - link "Peronists" [ref=e233] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peronism
            - text: ", although they never registered in the party, and she started her career as a singer for the"
            - link "Peronist Party" [ref=e234] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peronist_Party
            - text: in
            - link "Tucuman" [ref=e235] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Tucum%C3%A1n_Province
            - text: under the name Gladys Osorio.
            - superscript [ref=e236]:
              - link "[6]" [ref=e237] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-6"
            - text: In 1950, at age fifteen, she won a singing competition organized by a local radio station and was given a contract to perform for two months.
            - superscript [ref=e238]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e239] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: She recorded her first album,
            - link "La Voz de la Zafra" [ref=e241] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/La_voz_de_la_zafra
            - text: ", in 1959."
            - superscript [ref=e242]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e243] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: A performance at the 1965
            - link "Cosquín National Folklore Festival" [ref=e244] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cosqu%C3%ADn_Festival
            - text: —where she was introduced and brought to the stage while sitting in the audience by fellow folk singer
            - link "Jorge Cafrune" [ref=e245] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jorge_Cafrune
            - text: —
            - superscript [ref=e246]:
              - link "[8]" [ref=e247] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-test-8"
            - text: brought her to the attention of the Argentine public.
            - superscript [ref=e248]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e249] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: Sosa and her first husband,
            - link "Manuel Oscar Matus" [ref=e250] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /w/index.php?title=Manuel_Oscar_Matus&action=edit&redlink=1
            - text: ", with whom she had one son, were key players in the mid-60s"
            - link "nueva canción" [ref=e252] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nueva_canci%C3%B3n
            - text: movement (which was called nuevo cancionero in Argentina).
            - superscript [ref=e253]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e254] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: Her second record was Canciones con Fundamento, a collection of Argentine folk songs.
          - figure "Sosa with Félix Luna and Ariel Ramírez (at the piano)" [ref=e255]:
            - link [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Mercedes_Sosa,_F%C3%A9lix_Luna_y_Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez.jpg
              - img [ref=e257]
            - generic [ref=e258]:
              - text: Sosa with
              - link "Félix Luna" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/F%C3%A9lix_Luna
              - text: and
              - link "Ariel Ramírez" [ref=e260] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez
              - text: (at the piano)
          - paragraph [ref=e261]:
            - text: Sosa "spent the late 1960s building her audience in Europe and among the cosmopolitan middle class in Buenos Aires, becoming in the process a much bigger star" than her contemporaries.
            - superscript [ref=e262]:
              - link "[10]" [ref=e263] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-10"
            - text: In 1967, Sosa toured the United States and Europe with great success.
            - superscript [ref=e264]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e266] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
            - text: In later years, she performed and recorded extensively, broadening her repertoire to include material from throughout Latin America.
          - paragraph [ref=e267]:
            - text: In the early 1970s, Sosa released two concept albums in collaboration with composer
            - link "Ariel Ramírez" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez
            - text: and lyricist
            - link "Félix Luna" [ref=e269] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/F%C3%A9lix_Luna
            - text: ": Cantata Sudamericana and Mujeres Argentinas (Argentine Women). She also recorded a tribute to Chilean musician"
            - link "Violeta Parra" [ref=e270] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Violeta_Parra
            - text: in 1971, including what was to become one of Sosa's signature songs,
            - link "Gracias a la vida" [ref=e272] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gracias_a_la_vida
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e273]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - superscript [ref=e275]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e276] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-ap-11"
            - text: She further popularized of songs written by
            - link "Milton Nascimento" [ref=e277] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Milton_Nascimento
            - text: of Brazil and
            - link "Pablo Milanés" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pablo_Milan%C3%A9s
            - text: and
            - link "Silvio Rodríguez" [ref=e279] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Silvio_Rodr%C3%ADguez
            - text: both from
            - link "Cuba" [ref=e280] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cuba
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e281]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - text: Throughout the decade, she released albums such as Hasta la Victoria in 1972 and Traigo un Pueblo en mi Voz in 1973. They featured songs like "Cuando tenga la tierra", written by
            - link "Ariel Petrocelli" [ref=e283] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /w/index.php?title=Ariel_Petrocelli&action=edit&redlink=1
            - text: and Daniel Toro, which tackles political and social issues like wealth and land inequality.
            - superscript [ref=e284]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e285] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:2-12"
            - superscript [ref=e286]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e287] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-13"
            - text: During the 1970s she was a part of two films by the director
            - link "Leopoldo Torre Nilsson" [ref=e288] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leopoldo_Torre_Nilsson
            - text: ":"
            - link "El Santo de la Espada" [ref=e290] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/El_Santo_de_la_Espada
            - text: in 1970 and
            - link "Güemes, la tierra en armas" [ref=e292] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/G%C3%BCemes:_la_tierra_en_armas
            - text: in 1971, in which she portrayed
            - link "Juana Azurduy de Padilla" [ref=e293] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Juana_Azurduy_de_Padilla
            - text: ", the guerrilla military leader who fought for Argentine independence."
            - superscript [ref=e294]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e295] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:2-12"
            - superscript [ref=e296]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e297] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-14"
          - figure "Sosa in 1972" [ref=e298]:
            - link [ref=e299] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Mercedes_Sosa_2.jpg
              - img [ref=e300]
            - generic [ref=e301]: Sosa in 1972
          - paragraph [ref=e302]:
            - text: After the
            - link "military junta" [ref=e303] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/National_Reorganization_Process
            - text: of
            - link "Jorge Videla" [ref=e304] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jorge_Videla
            - text: came to power in 1976, the atmosphere in Argentina grew increasingly oppressive. Sosa faced death threats against both her and her family, but refused for many years to leave the country. At a concert in
            - link "La Plata" [ref=e305] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/La_Plata
            - text: in 1979, Sosa was searched and arrested on stage, along with all those attending the concert.
            - superscript [ref=e306]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e307] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: Their release came about through international intervention.
            - superscript [ref=e308]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e309] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: Despite attempts to hold more concerts, she was officially barred from performing by the military regime.
            - superscript [ref=e310]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e311] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: Banned in her own country, she moved to Paris and then to
            - link "Madrid" [ref=e312] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Madrid
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e313]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e314] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - superscript [ref=e315]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e316] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: She has spoken publicly about her artistic and emotional struggles during this period of her life.
            - superscript [ref=e317]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e318] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: While in exile, she released the album A Quien Doy in 1981. The album included a recording of the song "Cuando Me Acuerdo de Mi Pais" which was originally written by the prolific Chilean singer/songwriter,
            - link "Patricio Manns" [ref=e319] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Patricio_Manns
            - text: . The song, which he wrote while also in political exile, expresses the sorrow he felt from being separated from his homeland.
            - superscript [ref=e320]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e321] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-15"
            - text: She related to this feeling and struggled to continue recording and performing. In an interview with the New York Times, she said, “It was a mental problem, a problem of morale...It wasn’t my throat, or anything physical".
            - superscript [ref=e322]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e323] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

          - paragraph [ref=e277]:
            - text: Haydée Marta Mercedes Sosa Girón (9 July 1935
            - superscript [ref=e278]:
              - link "[1]" [ref=e279] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-birth-1"
            - text: – 4 October 2009) was an Argentine singer who was popular throughout
            - link "Latin America" [ref=e280] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_America
            - text: and many countries outside the region. With her roots in
            - link "Argentine folk music" [ref=e281] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Folk_music_of_Argentina
            - text: ", Sosa became one of the preeminent exponents of"
            - link "El nuevo cancionero" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nueva_canci%C3%B3n
            - text: . She gave voice to songs written by many Latin American songwriters. She was hailed as the "voice of the voiceless ones",
            - superscript [ref=e283]:
              - link "[2]" [ref=e284] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-tmc-2"
            - text: and often called "the conscience of Latin America".
            - superscript [ref=e285]:
              - link "[3]" [ref=e286] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Heckman-3"
          - paragraph [ref=e287]:
            - text: Sosa performed in venues such as the
            - link "Lincoln Center" [ref=e288] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lincoln_Center
            - text: in New York City, the
            - link "Théâtre Mogador" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_Mogador
            - text: in Paris, the
            - link "Sistine Chapel" [ref=e290] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sistine_Chapel
            - text: in Vatican City, as well as sold-out shows in New York's
            - link "Carnegie Hall" [ref=e291] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carnegie_Hall
            - text: and the Roman
            - link "Colosseum" [ref=e292] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Colosseum
            - text: during her final decade of life. Her career spanned four decades and she was the recipient of six
            - link "Latin Grammy" [ref=e293] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy
            - text: awards (2000, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2009, 2011), including a
            - link "Latin Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award" [ref=e294] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award
            - text: in 2004 and two posthumous
            - link "Latin Grammy Award for Best Folk Album" [ref=e295] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy_Award_for_Best_Folk_Album
            - text: in 2009 and 2011. She won the
            - link "Premio Gardel" [ref=e296] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Premios_Gardel
            - text: in 2000, the main musical award in Argentina. She served as an ambassador for
            - link "UNICEF" [ref=e297] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/UNICEF
            - text: .

            - superscript [ref=e308]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e309] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - text: Her nickname "la negra", which is a common nickname in Argentina for people with darker complexion, is a reference to her indigenous heritage.
            - superscript [ref=e310]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e311] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: Her parents, a day laborer and a washerwoman,
            - superscript [ref=e312]:
              - link "[3]" [ref=e313] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Heckman-3"
            - text: were
            - link "Peronists" [ref=e314] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", although they never registered in the party, and she started her career as a singer for the"
            - link "Peronist Party" [ref=e315] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: in
            - link "Tucuman" [ref=e316] [cursor=pointer]:

            - superscript [ref=e317]:
              - link "[6]" [ref=e318] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-6"
            - text: In 1950, at age fifteen, she won a singing competition organized by a local radio station and was given a contract to perform for two months.
            - superscript [ref=e319]:

            - superscript [ref=e323]:

            - superscript [ref=e327]:

            - superscript [ref=e329]:

            - text: Sosa and her first husband,
            - link "Manuel Oscar Matus" [ref=e331] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: movement (which was called nuevo cancionero in Argentina).
            - superscript [ref=e334]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e335] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: Her second record was Canciones con Fundamento, a collection of Argentine folk songs.

              - text: (at the piano)
          - paragraph [ref=e342]:
            - text: Sosa "spent the late 1960s building her audience in Europe and among the cosmopolitan middle class in Buenos Aires, becoming in the process a much bigger star" than her contemporaries.
            - superscript [ref=e343]:
              - link "[10]" [ref=e344] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-10"
            - text: In 1967, Sosa toured the United States and Europe with great success.
            - superscript [ref=e345]:

              - text: "]"

                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - text: Throughout the decade, she released albums such as Hasta la Victoria in 1972 and Traigo un Pueblo en mi Voz in 1973. They featured songs like "Cuando tenga la tierra", written by

            - superscript [ref=e365]:

            - superscript [ref=e367]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e368] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-13"
            - text: During the 1970s she was a part of two films by the director
            - link "Leopoldo Torre Nilsson" [ref=e369] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leopoldo_Torre_Nilsson
            - text: ":"
            - link "El Santo de la Espada" [ref=e371] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/El_Santo_de_la_Espada
            - text: in 1970 and
            - link "Güemes, la tierra en armas" [ref=e373] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/G%C3%BCemes:_la_tierra_en_armas
            - text: in 1971, in which she portrayed
            - link "Juana Azurduy de Padilla" [ref=e374] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Juana_Azurduy_de_Padilla
            - text: ", the guerrilla military leader who fought for Argentine independence."
            - superscript [ref=e375]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e376] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:2-12"
            - superscript [ref=e377]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e378] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-14"
          - figure "Sosa in 1972" [ref=e379]:
            - link [ref=e380] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Mercedes_Sosa_2.jpg
              - img [ref=e381]
            - generic [ref=e382]: Sosa in 1972
          - paragraph [ref=e383]:
            - text: After the
            - link "military junta" [ref=e384] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/National_Reorganization_Process
            - text: of
            - link "Jorge Videla" [ref=e385] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jorge_Videla
            - text: came to power in 1976, the atmosphere in Argentina grew increasingly oppressive. Sosa faced death threats against both her and her family, but refused for many years to leave the country. At a concert in
            - link "La Plata" [ref=e386] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/La_Plata
            - text: in 1979, Sosa was searched and arrested on stage, along with all those attending the concert.
            - superscript [ref=e387]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e388] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: Their release came about through international intervention.
            - superscript [ref=e389]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e390] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: Despite attempts to hold more concerts, she was officially barred from performing by the military regime.
            - superscript [ref=e391]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e392] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: Banned in her own country, she moved to Paris and then to
            - link "Madrid" [ref=e393] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Madrid
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e394]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e395] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - superscript [ref=e396]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e397] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: She has spoken publicly about her artistic and emotional struggles during this period of her life.
            - superscript [ref=e398]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e399] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: While in exile, she released the album A Quien Doy in 1981. The album included a recording of the song "Cuando Me Acuerdo de Mi Pais" which was originally written by the prolific Chilean singer/songwriter,
            - link "Patricio Manns" [ref=e400] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Patricio_Manns
            - text: . The song, which he wrote while also in political exile, expresses the sorrow he felt from being separated from his homeland.
            - superscript [ref=e401]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e402] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-15"
            - text: She related to this feeling and struggled to continue recording and performing. In an interview with the New York Times, she said, “It was a mental problem, a problem of morale...It wasn’t my throat, or anything physical".
            - superscript [ref=e403]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e404] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
          - paragraph [ref=e405]:
            - text: Sosa returned to Argentina from her exile in Europe in February 1982,
            - superscript [ref=e406]:
              - link "[16]" [ref=e407] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:1-16"
            - superscript [ref=e408]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e409] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: several months before the military regime collapsed as a result of the
            - link "Falklands War" [ref=e410] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Falklands_War
            - text: ", and gave a series of concerts at the"
            - link "Teatro Ópera" [ref=e412] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Teatro_Opera
            - text: in Buenos Aires, where she invited many of her younger colleagues to share the stage. A
            - link "double album" [ref=e413] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Double_album
            - text: of recordings,
            - generic [ref=e414]:
              - link "Mercedes Sosa en Argentina" [ref=e415] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Mercedes_Sosa_en_Argentina
              - text: ","
            - text: from these performances became an instant best seller. She then traveled to perform in her home province of Tucuman. However, these performances were largely ignored by mainstream media in the country.
            - superscript [ref=e416]:
              - link "[16]" [ref=e417] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:1-16"
            - text: In subsequent years, Sosa continued to tour both in Argentina and abroad, performing in such venues as the
            - link "Lincoln Center" [ref=e418] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lincoln_Center
            - text: in New York City and the
            - link "Théâtre Mogador" [ref=e420] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_Mogador
            - text: in Paris. In poor health for much of the 1990s, she performed a comeback show in Argentina in 1998.
            - superscript [ref=e421]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e422] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: In 1994, she played in the
            - link "Sistine Chapel" [ref=e423] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sistine_Chapel
            - text: in Vatican City.
            - superscript [ref=e424]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e425] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - text: In 2002, she sold out both
            - link "Carnegie Hall" [ref=e426] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carnegie_Hall
            - text: in New York and the
            - link "Colosseum" [ref=e427] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Colosseum
            - text: in Rome in the same year.
            - superscript [ref=e428]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"

          - paragraph [ref=e434]:
            - text: A supporter of
            - link "Perón" [ref=e435] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Juan_Per%C3%B3n
            - text: ", she favored leftist causes throughout her life. She supported President"
            - link "Raul Alfonsin" [ref=e436] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ra%C3%BAl_Alfons%C3%ADn
            - text: in the election of 1983 which marked the return of democracy in Argentina following the dictatorship. She referred to this election as "Argentina's Spring"
            - superscript [ref=e437]:
              - link "[17]" [ref=e438] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-17"
            - text: She opposed President
            - link "Carlos Menem" [ref=e439] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carlos_Menem
            - text: ", who was in office from 1989 to 1999, and supported the election of"
            - link "Néstor Kirchner" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/N%C3%A9stor_Kirchner
            - text: ", who became president in 2003."
            - superscript [ref=e441]:
              - link "[18]" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-18"
            - text: Sosa was a
            - link "UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/UNESCO_Goodwill_Ambassador
            - text: for Latin America and the Caribbean.
            - superscript [ref=e444]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - superscript [ref=e446]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-19"

            - text: Sosa disliked being identified as a protest singer.

            - superscript [ref=e451]:

            - text: Suffering from recurrent

            - superscript [ref=e544]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-29"
            - text: She died from
            - link "multiple organ failure" [ref=e546] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: on 4 October 2009, at 5:15 am.
            - superscript [ref=e547]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e548] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-ap-11"
            - text: She was survived by one son, Fabián Matus (d. 15 March 2019), born of her first marriage.
            - superscript [ref=e549]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e550] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - superscript [ref=e551]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_singer_Mercedes_Sosa,_'voice_of_Latin_America,'_dies_at_74-30"
            - text: "He said: \"She lived her 74 years to the fullest. She had done practically everything she wanted, she didn't have any type of barrier or any type of fear that limited her\"."

              - link "[30]" [ref=e554] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_singer_Mercedes_Sosa,_'voice_of_Latin_America,'_dies_at_74-30"

            - text: "Her website featured the following: \"Her undisputed talent, her honesty and her profound convictions leave a great legacy to future generations\"."

                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_folk_icon_Sosa_dies_at_74-32"

            - superscript [ref=e563]:

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

            - text: Haydée Marta Mercedes Sosa Girón (9 July 1935
            - superscript [ref=e278]:

            - text: – 4 October 2009) was an Argentine singer who was popular throughout

            - link "Argentine folk music" [ref=e281] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", Sosa became one of the preeminent exponents of"
            - link "El nuevo cancionero" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nueva_canci%C3%B3n
            - text: . She gave voice to songs written by many Latin American songwriters. She was hailed as the "voice of the voiceless ones",
            - superscript [ref=e283]:

            - text: and often called "the conscience of Latin America".
            - superscript [ref=e285]:
              - link "[3]" [ref=e286] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Heckman-3"
          - paragraph [ref=e287]:
            - text: Sosa performed in venues such as the
            - link "Lincoln Center" [ref=e288] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: in New York City, the
            - link "Théâtre Mogador" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: in Paris, the
            - link "Sistine Chapel" [ref=e290] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sistine_Chapel
            - text: in Vatican City, as well as sold-out shows in New York's
            - link "Carnegie Hall" [ref=e291] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carnegie_Hall
            - text: and the Roman
            - link "Colosseum" [ref=e292] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Colosseum
            - text: during her final decade of life. Her career spanned four decades and she was the recipient of six
            - link "Latin Grammy" [ref=e293] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy
            - text: awards (2000, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2009, 2011), including a
            - link "Latin Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award" [ref=e294] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award
            - text: in 2004 and two posthumous
            - link "Latin Grammy Award for Best Folk Album" [ref=e295] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy_Award_for_Best_Folk_Album
            - text: in 2009 and 2011. She won the
            - link "Premio Gardel" [ref=e296] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Premios_Gardel
            - text: in 2000, the main musical award in Argentina. She served as an ambassador for

            - superscript [ref=e310]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e311] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: Her parents, a day laborer and a washerwoman,
            - superscript [ref=e312]:

            - text: were

            - text: Sosa "spent the late 1960s building her audience in Europe and among the cosmopolitan middle class in Buenos Aires, becoming in the process a much bigger star" than her contemporaries.

                - /url: "#cite_note-13"
            - text: During the 1970s she was a part of two films by the director
            - link "Leopoldo Torre Nilsson" [ref=e369] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leopoldo_Torre_Nilsson
            - text: ":"
            - link "El Santo de la Espada" [ref=e371] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/El_Santo_de_la_Espada
            - text: in 1970 and
            - link "Güemes, la tierra en armas" [ref=e373] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/G%C3%BCemes:_la_tierra_en_armas
            - text: in 1971, in which she portrayed
            - link "Juana Azurduy de Padilla" [ref=e374] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Juana_Azurduy_de_Padilla
            - text: ", the guerrilla military leader who fought for Argentine independence."
            - superscript [ref=e375]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e376] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:2-12"
            - superscript [ref=e377]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e378] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-14"
          - figure "Sosa in 1972" [ref=e379]:
            - link [ref=e380] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Mercedes_Sosa_2.jpg
              - img [ref=e381]
            - generic [ref=e382]: Sosa in 1972
          - paragraph [ref=e383]:
            - text: After the
            - link "military junta" [ref=e384] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/National_Reorganization_Process
            - text: of
            - link "Jorge Videla" [ref=e385] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jorge_Videla
            - text: came to power in 1976, the atmosphere in Argentina grew increasingly oppressive. Sosa faced death threats against both her and her family, but refused for many years to leave the country. At a concert in
            - link "La Plata" [ref=e386] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/La_Plata
            - text: in 1979, Sosa was searched and arrested on stage, along with all those attending the concert.
            - superscript [ref=e387]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e388] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: Their release came about through international intervention.
            - superscript [ref=e389]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e390] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: Despite attempts to hold more concerts, she was officially barred from performing by the military regime.
            - superscript [ref=e391]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e392] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: Banned in her own country, she moved to Paris and then to
            - link "Madrid" [ref=e393] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Madrid
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e394]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e395] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - superscript [ref=e396]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e397] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: She has spoken publicly about her artistic and emotional struggles during this period of her life.
            - superscript [ref=e398]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e399] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: While in exile, she released the album A Quien Doy in 1981. The album included a recording of the song "Cuando Me Acuerdo de Mi Pais" which was originally written by the prolific Chilean singer/songwriter,
            - link "Patricio Manns" [ref=e400] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Patricio_Manns
            - text: . The song, which he wrote while also in political exile, expresses the sorrow he felt from being separated from his homeland.
            - superscript [ref=e401]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e402] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-15"
            - text: She related to this feeling and struggled to continue recording and performing. In an interview with the New York Times, she said, “It was a mental problem, a problem of morale...It wasn’t my throat, or anything physical".
            - superscript [ref=e403]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e404] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
          - paragraph [ref=e405]:
            - text: Sosa returned to Argentina from her exile in Europe in February 1982,
            - superscript [ref=e406]:
              - link "[16]" [ref=e407] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:1-16"
            - superscript [ref=e408]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e409] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: several months before the military regime collapsed as a result of the
            - link "Falklands War" [ref=e410] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Falklands_War
            - text: ", and gave a series of concerts at the"
            - link "Teatro Ópera" [ref=e412] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Teatro_Opera
            - text: in Buenos Aires, where she invited many of her younger colleagues to share the stage. A
            - link "double album" [ref=e413] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Double_album
            - text: of recordings,
            - generic [ref=e414]:
              - link "Mercedes Sosa en Argentina" [ref=e415] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Mercedes_Sosa_en_Argentina
              - text: ","
            - text: from these performances became an instant best seller. She then traveled to perform in her home province of Tucuman. However, these performances were largely ignored by mainstream media in the country.
            - superscript [ref=e416]:
              - link "[16]" [ref=e417] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:1-16"
            - text: In subsequent years, Sosa continued to tour both in Argentina and abroad, performing in such venues as the
            - link "Lincoln Center" [ref=e418] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lincoln_Center
            - text: in New York City and the
            - link "Théâtre Mogador" [ref=e420] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_Mogador
            - text: in Paris. In poor health for much of the 1990s, she performed a comeback show in Argentina in 1998.
            - superscript [ref=e421]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e422] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: In 1994, she played in the
            - link "Sistine Chapel" [ref=e423] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sistine_Chapel
            - text: in Vatican City.
            - superscript [ref=e424]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e425] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - text: In 2002, she sold out both
            - link "Carnegie Hall" [ref=e426] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carnegie_Hall
            - text: in New York and the
            - link "Colosseum" [ref=e427] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Colosseum
            - text: in Rome in the same year.
            - superscript [ref=e428]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"

          - paragraph [ref=e434]:
            - text: A supporter of
            - link "Perón" [ref=e435] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Juan_Per%C3%B3n
            - text: ", she favored leftist causes throughout her life. She supported President"
            - link "Raul Alfonsin" [ref=e436] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ra%C3%BAl_Alfons%C3%ADn
            - text: in the election of 1983 which marked the return of democracy in Argentina following the dictatorship. She referred to this election as "Argentina's Spring"
            - superscript [ref=e437]:
              - link "[17]" [ref=e438] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-17"
            - text: She opposed President
            - link "Carlos Menem" [ref=e439] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carlos_Menem
            - text: ", who was in office from 1989 to 1999, and supported the election of"
            - link "Néstor Kirchner" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/N%C3%A9stor_Kirchner
            - text: ", who became president in 2003."
            - superscript [ref=e441]:
              - link "[18]" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-18"
            - text: Sosa was a
            - link "UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/UNESCO_Goodwill_Ambassador
            - text: for Latin America and the Caribbean.
            - superscript [ref=e444]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - superscript [ref=e446]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-19"

            - text: Sosa disliked being identified as a protest singer.

            - superscript [ref=e451]:

            - text: Suffering from recurrent

            - superscript [ref=e544]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-29"
            - text: She died from
            - link "multiple organ failure" [ref=e546] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: on 4 October 2009, at 5:15 am.
            - superscript [ref=e547]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e548] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-ap-11"
            - text: She was survived by one son, Fabián Matus (d. 15 March 2019), born of her first marriage.
            - superscript [ref=e549]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e550] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - superscript [ref=e551]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_singer_Mercedes_Sosa,_'voice_of_Latin_America,'_dies_at_74-30"
            - text: "He said: \"She lived her 74 years to the fullest. She had done practically everything she wanted, she didn't have any type of barrier or any type of fear that limited her\"."

              - link "[30]" [ref=e554] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_singer_Mercedes_Sosa,_'voice_of_Latin_America,'_dies_at_74-30"

            - text: "Her website featured the following: \"Her undisputed talent, her honesty and her profound convictions leave a great legacy to future generations\"."

                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_folk_icon_Sosa_dies_at_74-32"

            - superscript [ref=e563]:

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

            - superscript [ref=e283]:

            - link "Théâtre Mogador" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: in Paris, the

            - text: in Vatican City, as well as sold-out shows in New York's
            - link "Carnegie Hall" [ref=e291] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and the Roman
            - link "Colosseum" [ref=e292] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Colosseum
            - text: during her final decade of life. Her career spanned four decades and she was the recipient of six
            - link "Latin Grammy" [ref=e293] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: awards (2000, 2003, 2004, 2006, 2009, 2011), including a
            - link "Latin Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award" [ref=e294] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy_Lifetime_Achievement_Award
            - text: in 2004 and two posthumous
            - link "Latin Grammy Award for Best Folk Album" [ref=e295] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Latin_Grammy_Award_for_Best_Folk_Album
            - text: in 2009 and 2011. She won the

            - text: in 2000, the main musical award in Argentina. She served as an ambassador for

            - text: During the 1970s she was a part of two films by the director
            - link "Leopoldo Torre Nilsson" [ref=e369] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leopoldo_Torre_Nilsson
            - text: ":"
            - link "El Santo de la Espada" [ref=e371] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/El_Santo_de_la_Espada
            - text: in 1970 and
            - link "Güemes, la tierra en armas" [ref=e373] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/G%C3%BCemes:_la_tierra_en_armas
            - text: in 1971, in which she portrayed
            - link "Juana Azurduy de Padilla" [ref=e374] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Juana_Azurduy_de_Padilla
            - text: ", the guerrilla military leader who fought for Argentine independence."
            - superscript [ref=e375]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e376] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:2-12"
            - superscript [ref=e377]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e378] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-14"
          - figure "Sosa in 1972" [ref=e379]:
            - link [ref=e380] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Mercedes_Sosa_2.jpg
              - img [ref=e381]
            - generic [ref=e382]: Sosa in 1972
          - paragraph [ref=e383]:
            - text: After the
            - link "military junta" [ref=e384] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/National_Reorganization_Process
            - text: of
            - link "Jorge Videla" [ref=e385] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jorge_Videla
            - text: came to power in 1976, the atmosphere in Argentina grew increasingly oppressive. Sosa faced death threats against both her and her family, but refused for many years to leave the country. At a concert in
            - link "La Plata" [ref=e386] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/La_Plata
            - text: in 1979, Sosa was searched and arrested on stage, along with all those attending the concert.
            - superscript [ref=e387]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e388] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: Their release came about through international intervention.
            - superscript [ref=e389]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e390] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: Despite attempts to hold more concerts, she was officially barred from performing by the military regime.
            - superscript [ref=e391]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e392] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: Banned in her own country, she moved to Paris and then to
            - link "Madrid" [ref=e393] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Madrid
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e394]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e395] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - superscript [ref=e396]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e397] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: She has spoken publicly about her artistic and emotional struggles during this period of her life.
            - superscript [ref=e398]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e399] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: While in exile, she released the album A Quien Doy in 1981. The album included a recording of the song "Cuando Me Acuerdo de Mi Pais" which was originally written by the prolific Chilean singer/songwriter,
            - link "Patricio Manns" [ref=e400] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Patricio_Manns
            - text: . The song, which he wrote while also in political exile, expresses the sorrow he felt from being separated from his homeland.
            - superscript [ref=e401]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e402] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-15"
            - text: She related to this feeling and struggled to continue recording and performing. In an interview with the New York Times, she said, “It was a mental problem, a problem of morale...It wasn’t my throat, or anything physical".
            - superscript [ref=e403]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e404] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
          - paragraph [ref=e405]:
            - text: Sosa returned to Argentina from her exile in Europe in February 1982,
            - superscript [ref=e406]:
              - link "[16]" [ref=e407] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:1-16"
            - superscript [ref=e408]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e409] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: several months before the military regime collapsed as a result of the
            - link "Falklands War" [ref=e410] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Falklands_War
            - text: ", and gave a series of concerts at the"
            - link "Teatro Ópera" [ref=e412] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Teatro_Opera
            - text: in Buenos Aires, where she invited many of her younger colleagues to share the stage. A
            - link "double album" [ref=e413] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Double_album
            - text: of recordings,
            - generic [ref=e414]:
              - link "Mercedes Sosa en Argentina" [ref=e415] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Mercedes_Sosa_en_Argentina
              - text: ","
            - text: from these performances became an instant best seller. She then traveled to perform in her home province of Tucuman. However, these performances were largely ignored by mainstream media in the country.
            - superscript [ref=e416]:
              - link "[16]" [ref=e417] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:1-16"
            - text: In subsequent years, Sosa continued to tour both in Argentina and abroad, performing in such venues as the
            - link "Lincoln Center" [ref=e418] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lincoln_Center
            - text: in New York City and the
            - link "Théâtre Mogador" [ref=e420] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_Mogador
            - text: in Paris. In poor health for much of the 1990s, she performed a comeback show in Argentina in 1998.
            - superscript [ref=e421]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e422] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: In 1994, she played in the
            - link "Sistine Chapel" [ref=e423] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sistine_Chapel
            - text: in Vatican City.
            - superscript [ref=e424]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e425] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - text: In 2002, she sold out both
            - link "Carnegie Hall" [ref=e426] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carnegie_Hall
            - text: in New York and the
            - link "Colosseum" [ref=e427] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Colosseum
            - text: in Rome in the same year.
            - superscript [ref=e428]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"

          - paragraph [ref=e434]:
            - text: A supporter of
            - link "Perón" [ref=e435] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Juan_Per%C3%B3n
            - text: ", she favored leftist causes throughout her life. She supported President"
            - link "Raul Alfonsin" [ref=e436] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ra%C3%BAl_Alfons%C3%ADn
            - text: in the election of 1983 which marked the return of democracy in Argentina following the dictatorship. She referred to this election as "Argentina's Spring"
            - superscript [ref=e437]:
              - link "[17]" [ref=e438] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-17"
            - text: She opposed President
            - link "Carlos Menem" [ref=e439] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", who was in office from 1989 to 1999, and supported the election of"
            - link "Néstor Kirchner" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/N%C3%A9stor_Kirchner
            - text: ", who became president in 2003."
            - superscript [ref=e441]:
              - link "[18]" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-18"
            - text: Sosa was a
            - link "UNESCO Goodwill Ambassador" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: for Latin America and the Caribbean.
            - superscript [ref=e444]:

            - superscript [ref=e446]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-19"

            - text: Suffering from recurrent

                - /url: "#cite_note-29"
            - text: She died from
            - link "multiple organ failure" [ref=e546] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: on 4 October 2009, at 5:15 am.
            - superscript [ref=e547]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e548] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-ap-11"
            - text: She was survived by one son, Fabián Matus (d. 15 March 2019), born of her first marriage.
            - superscript [ref=e549]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e550] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - superscript [ref=e551]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_singer_Mercedes_Sosa,_'voice_of_Latin_America,'_dies_at_74-30"
            - text: "He said: \"She lived her 74 years to the fullest. She had done practically everything she wanted, she didn't have any type of barrier or any type of fear that limited her\"."

              - link "[30]" [ref=e554] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_singer_Mercedes_Sosa,_'voice_of_Latin_America,'_dies_at_74-30"

                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_folk_legend_Mercedes_Sosa_dead_at_74-31"
            - text: "Her website featured the following: \"Her undisputed talent, her honesty and her profound convictions leave a great legacy to future generations\"."

                - /url: "#cite_note-Argentine_folk_icon_Sosa_dies_at_74-32"

            - text: Her nickname "la negra", which is a common nickname in Argentina for people with darker complexion, is a reference to her indigenous heritage.
            - superscript [ref=e310]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e311] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: Her parents, a day laborer and a washerwoman,
            - superscript [ref=e312]:

            - text: were
            - link "Peronists" [ref=e314] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", although they never registered in the party, and she started her career as a singer for the"
            - link "Peronist Party" [ref=e315] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: in
            - link "Tucuman" [ref=e316] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: under the name Gladys Osorio.
            - superscript [ref=e317]:
              - link "[6]" [ref=e318] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-6"
            - text: In 1950, at age fifteen, she won a singing competition organized by a local radio station and was given a contract to perform for two months.
            - superscript [ref=e319]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e320] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: She recorded her first album,
            - link "La Voz de la Zafra" [ref=e322] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/La_voz_de_la_zafra
            - text: ", in 1959."
            - superscript [ref=e323]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e324] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: A performance at the 1965
            - link "Cosquín National Folklore Festival" [ref=e325] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cosqu%C3%ADn_Festival
            - text: —where she was introduced and brought to the stage while sitting in the audience by fellow folk singer
            - link "Jorge Cafrune" [ref=e326] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: —
            - superscript [ref=e327]:

            - text: brought her to the attention of the Argentine public.
            - superscript [ref=e329]:

            - text: Sosa and her first husband,
            - link "Manuel Oscar Matus" [ref=e331] [cursor=pointer]:

              - /url: /wiki/Nueva_canci%C3%B3n
            - text: movement (which was called nuevo cancionero in Argentina).
            - superscript [ref=e334]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e335] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: Her second record was Canciones con Fundamento, a collection of Argentine folk songs.

              - text: (at the piano)
          - paragraph [ref=e342]:
            - text: Sosa "spent the late 1960s building her audience in Europe and among the cosmopolitan middle class in Buenos Aires, becoming in the process a much bigger star" than her contemporaries.
            - superscript [ref=e343]:
              - link "[10]" [ref=e344] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-10"
            - text: In 1967, Sosa toured the United States and Europe with great success.
            - superscript [ref=e345]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e347] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
            - text: In later years, she performed and recorded extensively, broadening her repertoire to include material from throughout Latin America.
          - paragraph [ref=e348]:
            - text: In the early 1970s, Sosa released two concept albums in collaboration with composer
            - link "Ariel Ramírez" [ref=e349] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ariel_Ram%C3%ADrez
            - text: and lyricist
            - link "Félix Luna" [ref=e350] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/F%C3%A9lix_Luna
            - text: ": Cantata Sudamericana and Mujeres Argentinas (Argentine Women). She also recorded a tribute to Chilean musician"
            - link "Violeta Parra" [ref=e351] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Violeta_Parra
            - text: in 1971, including what was to become one of Sosa's signature songs,
            - link "Gracias a la vida" [ref=e353] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gracias_a_la_vida
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e354]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e355] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - superscript [ref=e356]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e357] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-ap-11"
            - text: She further popularized of songs written by
            - link "Milton Nascimento" [ref=e358] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Milton_Nascimento
            - text: of Brazil and
            - link "Pablo Milanés" [ref=e359] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pablo_Milan%C3%A9s
            - text: and
            - link "Silvio Rodríguez" [ref=e360] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Silvio_Rodr%C3%ADguez
            - text: both from
            - link "Cuba" [ref=e361] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cuba
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e362]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e363] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - text: Throughout the decade, she released albums such as Hasta la Victoria in 1972 and Traigo un Pueblo en mi Voz in 1973. They featured songs like "Cuando tenga la tierra", written by
            - link "Ariel Petrocelli" [ref=e364] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /w/index.php?title=Ariel_Petrocelli&action=edit&redlink=1
            - text: and Daniel Toro, which tackles political and social issues like wealth and land inequality.
            - superscript [ref=e365]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e366] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:2-12"
            - superscript [ref=e367]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e368] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-13"
            - text: During the 1970s she was a part of two films by the director
            - link "Leopoldo Torre Nilsson" [ref=e369] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leopoldo_Torre_Nilsson
            - text: ":"
            - link "El Santo de la Espada" [ref=e371] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/El_Santo_de_la_Espada
            - text: in 1970 and
            - link "Güemes, la tierra en armas" [ref=e373] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/G%C3%BCemes:_la_tierra_en_armas
            - text: in 1971, in which she portrayed
            - link "Juana Azurduy de Padilla" [ref=e374] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Juana_Azurduy_de_Padilla
            - text: ", the guerrilla military leader who fought for Argentine independence."
            - superscript [ref=e375]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e376] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:2-12"
            - superscript [ref=e377]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e378] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-14"
          - figure "Sosa in 1972" [ref=e379]:
            - link [ref=e380] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Mercedes_Sosa_2.jpg
              - img [ref=e381]
            - generic [ref=e382]: Sosa in 1972
          - paragraph [ref=e383]:
            - text: After the
            - link "military junta" [ref=e384] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/National_Reorganization_Process
            - text: of
            - link "Jorge Videla" [ref=e385] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Jorge_Videla
            - text: came to power in 1976, the atmosphere in Argentina grew increasingly oppressive. Sosa faced death threats against both her and her family, but refused for many years to leave the country. At a concert in
            - link "La Plata" [ref=e386] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/La_Plata
            - text: in 1979, Sosa was searched and arrested on stage, along with all those attending the concert.
            - superscript [ref=e387]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e388] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: Their release came about through international intervention.
            - superscript [ref=e389]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e390] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: Despite attempts to hold more concerts, she was officially barred from performing by the military regime.
            - superscript [ref=e391]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e392] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: Banned in her own country, she moved to Paris and then to
            - link "Madrid" [ref=e393] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Madrid
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e394]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e395] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - superscript [ref=e396]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e397] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: She has spoken publicly about her artistic and emotional struggles during this period of her life.
            - superscript [ref=e398]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e399] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
            - text: While in exile, she released the album A Quien Doy in 1981. The album included a recording of the song "Cuando Me Acuerdo de Mi Pais" which was originally written by the prolific Chilean singer/songwriter,
            - link "Patricio Manns" [ref=e400] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Patricio_Manns
            - text: . The song, which he wrote while also in political exile, expresses the sorrow he felt from being separated from his homeland.
            - superscript [ref=e401]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e402] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-15"
            - text: She related to this feeling and struggled to continue recording and performing. In an interview with the New York Times, she said, “It was a mental problem, a problem of morale...It wasn’t my throat, or anything physical".
            - superscript [ref=e403]:
              - link "[5]" [ref=e404] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:0-5"
          - paragraph [ref=e405]:
            - text: Sosa returned to Argentina from her exile in Europe in February 1982,
            - superscript [ref=e406]:
              - link "[16]" [ref=e407] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:1-16"
            - superscript [ref=e408]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e409] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Latin_artist_Mercedes_Sosa_dies-9"
            - text: several months before the military regime collapsed as a result of the
            - link "Falklands War" [ref=e410] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Falklands_War
            - text: ", and gave a series of concerts at the"
            - link "Teatro Ópera" [ref=e412] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Teatro_Opera
            - text: in Buenos Aires, where she invited many of her younger colleagues to share the stage. A
            - link "double album" [ref=e413] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Double_album
            - text: of recordings,
            - generic [ref=e414]:
              - link "Mercedes Sosa en Argentina" [ref=e415] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Mercedes_Sosa_en_Argentina
              - text: ","
            - text: from these performances became an instant best seller. She then traveled to perform in her home province of Tucuman. However, these performances were largely ignored by mainstream media in the country.
            - superscript [ref=e416]:
              - link "[16]" [ref=e417] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-:1-16"
            - text: In subsequent years, Sosa continued to tour both in Argentina and abroad, performing in such venues as the
            - link "Lincoln Center" [ref=e418] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lincoln_Center
            - text: in New York City and the
            - link "Théâtre Mogador" [ref=e420] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Th%C3%A9%C3%A2tre_Mogador
            - text: in Paris. In poor health for much of the 1990s, she performed a comeback show in Argentina in 1998.
            - superscript [ref=e421]:
              - link "[7]" [ref=e422] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Mercedes_Sosa:_Obituary-7"
            - text: In 1994, she played in the
            - link "Sistine Chapel" [ref=e423] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sistine_Chapel
            - text: in Vatican City.
            - superscript [ref=e424]:
              - link "[4]" [ref=e425] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"
            - text: In 2002, she sold out both
            - link "Carnegie Hall" [ref=e426] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carnegie_Hall
            - text: in New York and the
            - link "Colosseum" [ref=e427] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Colosseum
            - text: in Rome in the same year.

              - link "[4]" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Legendary_folk_singer_Mercedes_Sosa_dies_at_74-4"

            - text: A supporter of
            - link "Perón" [ref=e435] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", she favored leftist causes throughout her life. She supported President"
            - link "Raul Alfonsin" [ref=e436] [cursor=pointer]:
